#5049. The Best Watches for Men in 2026, Worn and Reviewed by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From fashion-forward watches to tough outdoor timepieces, we found the best watches for every budget.

THERE IS, PERHAPS, no menswear staple more classic than the wristwatch. Take Koon's gold watch in Pulp Fiction or 007's high-tech timepieces: The best watches for men tell a story and time, while instantly elevating your ensemble. In the watch world, there's a ticker for everyone—whether you're making power moves in the boardroom or chasing the next adventure. Need a leather-strapped dress watch that pairs nicely with your suit? Or maybe you're after a rugged outdoor watch or sports watch to track your laps?

With many options on the market, finding the right one can feel like diving into a black hole. But don't sweat it—we've tested it all, from everyday essentials to luxury standouts. Whether you're looking to monitor your fitness stats, are after your first watch to wear to the office, need some water-resistance, or have to have dial luminescence in the dark for easy readability, these 7 watches have proven to be the best in style, durability, and function. Step right up, because there's a watch for every guy.

Timex offers the ultimate bang-for-your-buck watch, no question about it. Our testers found it’s the easiest dial to read of all the watch options on this list. That lively blue is sharp enough to catch everyone’s attention but still versatile enough to pair with pretty much any casual or formal fit. It fits comfortably on the wrist and can smoothly adjust if you need to loosen or tighten it. And here’s the kicker: It’s under $100.

Yep, you get all this without putting a dent in your wallet—which can be said for nearly all the watches Timex makes. At the push of the crown, the brand's signature Indiglo light-up feature will take over, which means no squinting to see the time for both daytime strolls and late-night outings. The two-tone silver and brass case and mineral glass crystal keep it durable yet lightweight, so it can handle daily wear. Plus, with 10 different colorways, there are options to match your vibe, whether you want something that is "in your face" or semi-low-key.

Read More: The Best Amazon Watches for Men

Seiko delivers a solid mashup of modern and vintage flair in its special edition 5 Sports timepiece. Pulling inspo from the post-war racing boom of the 1960s, the watch dons a checkered flag bezel design, which is not something you see every day. The black dial continues the retro vibes with a white and black checkered circle to frame the indices for the numbers. We also love the red-orange second hand that adds a fun pop of color and harkens back to racing watches and timers of the post-war era.

Flip it over, and you’ve got a see-through caseback that lets you peek at the Caliber 4R36 movement—always a cool feature for anyone who loves the horology. We found it has some significant weight to it, but feels balanced and secure on the wrist. It’s an automatic watch, which means no batteries—you just wear it, and it powers itself through your every movement (approximately 41 hours of power reserve). Another bonus: It’s priced at a level that won’t make your wallet cry, which is a steal for the quality you’re getting—something Seiko has become known for.

Attention athletes and adventurers: The G-Shock G-LIDE is loaded with features that keep a record of your progress. First, this bad boy connects to a smartphone app that tracks tides at thousands of beaches, so it’s perfect for surfers, swimmers, or anyone who spends more time in the water than on land. I’ve used it at the pool during the summer, and it crushed it—handled constant splashes without a hiccup, shrugged off chlorine like it was nothing, and the resin strap stayed super comfortable even when wet. Not to mention, timing my laps was a total breeze. All to be expected for the legendary durability of G-Shocks.

In terms of fit, this one islarger, and on smaller wrists, it might look oversized or feel bulky. However, it's an athletic watch, so you'll probably be in workout shirts and not have to worry about fitting it under shirt cuffs.

All things considered, the G-Shock G-LIDE is brimming with other functions that track your laps, cadence, and pace—advantageous for runners, rowers, or gym-goers looking to crush their 2026 (and forthcoming 2027) goals. It’s designed to handle impacts (like any G-Shock), whether you’re wiping out on a wave or accidentally dropping it during a workout. I also found the LED backlight makes it super easy to read in low-light conditions, especially during a late-night jog. Other practical elements include a full auto-calendar, an energy-saving feature to keep the battery going strong, and a design that delivers durability and performance in one.

When it comes to field watches, the Hamilton Khaki Field is the gold standard—simple, robust, and packed with style. Speaking of which, the cool blue dial of this version, paired with the brushed steel case, gives it a clean, understated look that’s perfect for everyday wear. At 38mm, it’s compact and classic, sitting just right on your wrist without feeling too bulky.

Recreating the 1960s soldier watch, it’s a timepiece that nails that balance between functionality and style—you could wear it while exploring the outdoors or just heading to a casual dinner. The Super-LumiNova coating on the hands and markers is a game-changer, ensuring the watch is legible in low light or total darkness. We've put it to use during a camping trip and it lit up like a champ when the campfire died down, making it easy to check the time without fumbling for a flashlight. And just last year, Hamilton came out with a quartz version of the KF that's even more affordable and offers the ease of quartz.

The Bremont Terra Nova is the kind of watch that effortlessly blends rugged practicality with standout style. The cushion-shaped case? It’s got a cool military-meets-modern vibe that makes it stand out without trying too hard. Pair that with the rich green and black striped NATO strap, and you’ve got a watch that screams adventure but still looks sharp enough to wear out on the town.

As for the automatic movement, it features a Glucydur balance wheel (enhances its precision by maintaining consistent oscillations), an Anachron balance spring (offers excellent resistance to magnetic fields), and a Nivaflex mainspring (stores 38 hours of energy to power the watch).

What really makes it a go-to for adventurers and aviators is the oversized Super-LumiNova numerals. These bad boys light up like a beacon, so whether you’re navigating a trail at sunset or checking the time mid-flight in low light, you’ll always have clear visibility. It’s built for people who don’t just sit still—this is a watch designed to keep up with your wildest days and nights while keeping you looking sharp.

The Tudor Black Bay isn’t just any watch—it’s the perfect blend of timeless style, top-notch craftsmanship, and everyday usability. Let’s start with that 41mm steel case. The polished and brushed finish gives it that sophisticated edge while staying tough enough to manage the wear and tear of daily life. Paired with a black rubber strap, it strikes the perfect balance: sporty yet versatile, rugged yet refined. In other words, you could take it to the boardroom, the beach, or the mountains and it’ll look right at home. Not to mention, the strap has a slimmer profile and slightly textured feel that grips your wrist just enough without being sticky or uncomfortable. It's not overly thick or flimsy, and it doesn't soak water or sweat.

Tudor is known for its no-nonsense approach to legibility, and we found the Black Bay is no exception. It’s bold and clean, with luminous markers that practicality glow in low light. So whether you’re checking the time in a dimly lit bar or on an overnight hike, it’s always easy to read. Most mechanical watches offer approximately between 36 and 48 hours, but this one takes it up a level with a 70-hour power reserve. Overall, it’s the kind of watch that will still feel relevant and stylish 20, 30, and even 50 years down the road.

If you’re ready for any action-packed adventure—007 style—the Omega Seamaster Diver 300m is the watch you want. This model is the exact one Bond wears in "No Time to Die," so you know it’s got that "mission-ready" vibe. It’s super lightweight, made from titanium, and has a matching titanium mesh bracelet, so it’s built to last and handle anything—from magnetic fields to pressure underwater. Plus, it even has a Helium escape valve—a small pressure-release system that lets tiny built-up gas particles flee to prevent the crystal from popping off.

During our testing, we noticed the titanium bracelet feels incredibly light on the wrist, which makes a big difference for all-day comfort. It has a smooth, almost silky texture but isn't as glossy. Another bonus: Titanium is hypoallergenic, so it won't irritate the skin for people with metal sensitivities.

This watch is a serious upgrade and, yeah, it’s the priciest one on the list, but here’s why it’s worth the investment: It’s a timeless classic with next-level features that will last a lifetime. It’s powered by the Chronometer 8806 movement, so it’s super accurate, and it comes with a 5-year warranty, just in case. In all honesty, it's the kind of watch that'll make you look like a million bucks at an upscale gala or extravagant dinner party. Pair it with a tailored suit and some slick dress shoes for a look that means business.

The movement is the engine of the watch—it's what keeps it ticking. Below, we've broken down the main three types and their benefits.

Powered by a battery and known for being super accurate, quartz movement is low maintenance, lightweight, and affordable. It's a great option if you just want a reliable watch without the fuss. Quartz watches will only require the replacement of the battery every few years, which is a simple task and costs fairly little.

Backed by the motion of your wrist—no battery required. The gears that make up the movement wind themselves when the watch moves. Automatic watches feel a little more special, sometimes like high-end brands Rolex or Omega, but they'll need to be worn regularly or placed in a watch winder to stay powered. They'll also require consistent maintenance and servicing to keep them optimally running. Automatic watches typically cost more than most quartz watches, but there are many great options that are affordable these days.

You wind it yourself, usually every couple days. Instead of the movement rotating automatically with motion, the gears need hand-winding to keep the movement running. These watches require attention and typically harken back to the era of vintage, throwback timepieces like pocket watches. Manual watches usually cost more than quartz watches and are on par in price with some automatic watches. They tend to be a little less affordable though.

Think of the case as the body of the watch—it's the shell that houses everything important, like the movement (the engine that makes it tick) and the dial (the thing with the numbers and hands). Cases come in different shapes, sizes, and materials. Below, we break down the most common materials used for cases.

Durable, versatile, and scratch-resistant. It's the most common and works for everyday wear.

Lighter than steel but just as strong, making it perfect for sports watches.

Scratch-proof and sleek but can be a bit pricey. It has a modern, luxurious feel.

A strap is any flexible band—made of leather, rubber, nylon, or fabric—that secures the watch to your wrist. Straps can change the entire vibe of the watch. A bracelet, on the other hand, is made of metal—stainless steel, titanium, or sometimes gold—linked together. Bracelets usually feel sturdier and add a bit of weight to the watch, giving a more premium, polished look. The good thing is many watches allow you to swap between a strap and a bracelet, so you can switch up the style depending on the occasion.

Classic, comfortable, and stylish. Perfect for dress watches but less durable for heavy-duty activities.

Stainless steel or titanium bracelets are durable and versatile for both casual and formal occasions.

Great for sports and water activities—comfortable and easy to clean.

When shopping for the best men's watch, features and complications can make all the difference in terms of functionality and style. Ultimately, these details should match your lifestyle. We've broken down some important specs to keep an eye out for, but these are by no means an exhaustive list of everything you could find in some complex watches.

This is the ring around the watch face, and when it rotates, it actually serves a purpose (beyond looking cool). On dive watches, for example, the bezel is used to track elapsed time—turn it to line up with the minute hand before you dive, and you'll know how long you're underwater. Some bezels work for other things, like GMT watches, where they help track a second time zone. But in everyday life, most people just fidget with them because it's oddly satisfying with a ratcheting sound.

Water resistance tells you how well your watch can handle moisture. There are two equivalent measurements you will typically find when it comes to this rating. Meters (as in depth) is the first and atmosphere (designated as ATM and measures the pressure of every 10 meters. So the first rating is 30m, which is rated at 3 ATM. This is splash-proof, which means your watch can handle occasional hand-washing or light rain, but don't submerge it. 50m (5 ATM) is good for shallow water activities like light swimming, but no diving. 100m (10 ATM) can handle swimming, snorkeling, and most water sports. 200m+ (20 ATM) is built for diving and serious water activities. Watches like the Omega Seamaster are built specifically for this sort of pressure.

A chronograph is a type of complication added to the watch movement that essentially gives the watch a stopwatch functionality. It's great for timing events, workouts, or even laps around a track. You'll typically see sub dials for seconds, minutes, and sometimes hours. While it adds functionality, it also gives the watch a sporty, complex look. The most famous example of a chronograph is the Rolex Daytona, made famous by watch icon Paul Newman.

A date window adds convenience—you won't have to check your phone or calendar to know the date. It's a small but handy detail, especially for busy schedules. Watches such as the Seiko 5 or Tudor Black Bay makes this feature feel seamless by blending it into the design.

Luminous markers or hands are a must if you plan on wearing the watch in low-light situations, like at night or in darker environments. Watches with Super-LumiNova or tritium tubes glow brightly and for extended periods and make the dial easier to read when overhead light is sparse.

Pay attention to case diameter and thickness. Case diameter is the main number you'll see alongside watches. Generally speaking, around 38-42mm diameter is ideal for most wrists, but larger or smaller watches can suit personal taste. The diameter of cases tends to ebb and flow with watch trends. For the first part of this century, case sizes gravitated over 40mm for lots of watch makers. But in 2026, smaller watches (even down to 32 and 34mm) are en vogue. We like to find a happy medium and suggest trying on different sizes to see what's most comfortable for your wrist.

If you’re rough on your gear or are looking for an everyday wear, opt for a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal (the transparent covering that protects the dial), shock resistance, or robust designs for long-lasting wear.

Our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, continually tests almost every watch known to man and put them through their paces for everything they’re designed to handle: marathon training, cycling, traveling, hiking, sleep tracking, daily fitness routines, and dressy occasions. To identify the most ubiquitous watches, we relied on our previous experience testing and owning various models, as well as prior expert coverage on Men’s Health.

We considered features such as case material, comfort, battery life, accuracy, dial design and aesthetics, water resistance, and magnetic resistance. Bonus points were given for unique specs that added functionality like a date window or sub dials. Our picks aren't just utilitarian though—they're seriously stylish, making them the perfect accessory for everything from the gym to date nights. In the end, we narrowed it down to 7 standout watches that tick all the right boxes and can provide a timepiece for any type of guy.

#5046. Senators want state-licensed firms to keep issuing stablecoins after Jan. 18

Six senators are asking Treasury to let qualifying issuers keep issuing stablecoins while federal regulators review their states’ rules. The GENIUS Act takes effect Jan. 18, 2027.

Six senators are asking Treasury to let qualifying state-regulated stablecoin issuers keep putting new tokens into circulation while their states’ rules are under federal review. The GENIUS Act takes effect on January 18, 2027. Treasury’s proposal recognizes temporary relief for eligible federal applicants that get a waiver. It leaves open what happens if a state’s regulatory framework still awaits certification.

Sens. Cynthia Lummis and Kirsten Gillibrand led the bipartisan November 17 letter, which Lummis’s office released November 18. They asked Treasury for temporary protection during certification for issuers in states that will have a qualifying framework in place before January 18, 2028. They warned that a clearer federal route could steer issuers toward a federal license.

The proposed Section 3 rule would recognize relief for two groups with applications pending when the law takes effect. One is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution whose parent has applied on its behalf. The other is an applicant seeking to become a federally qualified payment stablecoin issuer. The primary federal regulator must grant a waiver, and its terms must cover the relevant Section 3 restriction. Relief can run for up to 12 months from the law’s effective date.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has a separate final rule that requires a written request and a substantially complete issuer application pending on or before January 18, 2027. It can grant relief on public-interest grounds or in extraordinary circumstances. Its licensing page says it has yet to open applications or waiver requests and is awaiting clearance for its application forms.

Treasury’s proposal treats the first transfer that gives someone outside the issuer the right to use, transfer or redeem the token as issuance. An issuer could create tokens for its own inventory and still face a restriction when it tries to put those tokens into circulation.

The OCC waiver rule gives active issuers a route to request temporary relief before the January deadline.

Treasury asked whether issuers should get relief before a state files for certification or while a review is pending. Four state regulatory and legislative groups asked for such protection in October. New York’s Department of Financial Services offered a different reading. It says qualifying issuers can keep issuing if their state’s rules are substantially similar and the state files within a year, until any final denial. It wants Treasury to confirm that reading in the final rule.

In the preamble to its interim rule, the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee described the state option for issuers with $10 billion or less in consolidated outstanding stablecoin issuance as requiring a state filing and committee approval. The committee has 30 days to decide once a complete certification has been submitted. It will seek to expedite initial reviews after the Act takes effect for states that had a qualifying regime in place by January 14, 2026. New York says it expects to qualify for expedited review. The initial state filing is due within a year of the Act taking effect.

The committee says it will start accepting certifications once the forms clear federal review. The paperwork record still shows the certification forms under review. If Treasury treats committee approval as a prerequisite and offers no temporary relief, issuers that depend on the state route could have to wait to issue new units.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Treasury’s proposal recognizes express federal waivers. It leaves the treatment of issuers under pending state certifications open.

A January pause could affect new supply before the general platform-sales rule applies.

Foreign-issued stablecoins face separate platform requirements from January 18, 2027.

The two branches map the federal waiver in proposed § 1523.4(a) and Treasury’s question about relief while state certification is pending. New York’s legal reading comes from its October 5 comment. The dates are statutory milestones.

Foreign-issued stablecoins face separate platform requirements from January 18, 2027.

New York’s approvals show why the legal issuer matters. The state’s Greenlist and charter register identify Ripple USD (RLUSD) and WisdomTree Dollar (USDW) as approved for issuance in the state. Ripple’s November 16 terms name Ripple Custody & Trust Co., the trade name of New York-chartered Standard Custody & Trust Company, LLC, as the RLUSD issuer.

The OCC charter record shows that Ripple National Trust Bank’s charter became effective October 26. Ripple said Standard Custody would continue issuing RLUSD, with the separate national bank authorized to manage reserves and provide custody.

WisdomTree identifies a different New York trust, WisdomTree Digital Trust Company, LLC, as USDW’s issuer. For either coin, a federal waiver would have to cover issuance by the legal issuer.

ZUSD still appears on the Greenlist. Its issuer, GMO-Z.com Trust Company, Inc., removed the mint function in May during a voluntary wind-down. The issuer said direct redemptions ended November 11 and that remaining balances are subject to mandatory redemption. ZUSD’s wind-down was already underway months before Treasury published its proposal.

Under the GENIUS Act, January 18, 2027 is the effective date for the U.S. issuance restriction. If a state-regulated issuer has to pause, the immediate effect would be on its ability to supply fresh units to customers and distributors. Trading already-issued tokens and redeeming them with the issuer are separate activities.

Starting July 18, 2028, digital asset service providers such as exchanges generally can offer or sell payment stablecoins to people in the U.S. only if the issuer is permitted or an exception applies.

A separate foreign-issuer provision applies from the Act’s effective date. It conditions U.S. platform availability on the foreign issuer’s ability and commitment to comply with lawful orders and reciprocal arrangements. Section 18 also provides a route for foreign issuers from comparable regimes that register with the OCC and meet other conditions.

#5045. How to Do the Walking Lunge for Lower Body Gains

Build stronger quads, hamstrings, and glutes one step at a time.

YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping. So why do most go-to leg exercises have you planting your feet in one spot?

Enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts. (A bonus: It’s a unilateral exercise that isn’t the dreaded Bulgarian split squat.) The walking lunge is one of the few strength moves that truly gets you moving. And in doing so, it exposes muscle imbalances, trains balance and coordination, and challenges your core and upper body more than you might expect—all while attacking every muscle in your legs.

Walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before. And in truth, they can be simple. Here, Men’s Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. walks you through the steps to take so that you’re not dragging your feet but making gains toward powerful legs.

FORM IS EVERYTHING with this move. You’ll want to stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, squeeze your glutes and shoulder blades while keeping your gaze at a neutral spot straight ahead of you.

Once you’re comfortable with this slow and controlled movement, you can add weights to build extra muscle and strength. You can hold them at your sides, hold them by your shoulders in what’s called a front rack position, or grab one heavy dumbbell and hold it to your chest in a goblet position. “Regardless of how you hold the load, make sure to keep your upper-body tight,” says Samuel. “Grip the dumbbells like you mean it, squeeze your shoulder blades, and tighten your abs, too.”

Don’t obsess over keeping your torso too upright, though, says Samuel. “Especially as you work with heavier loads, don’t be afraid to lean forward slightly,” he says. “That can help you capitalize on your glutes, one of your strongest muscle groups, with each stride.”

When you’re starting out, says Samuel, aim to take a step that keeps your front shin perpendicular to the ground when you lower your torso into the lunge. But as you grow more experienced, you can play with the length of your stride to chase different goals. “If you take very small steps forward,” says Samuel, “you’ll attack your quads more. Larger steps can help you build hip mobility and knee health. If you take larger steps, go lighter with the load.”

“The greatest benefits of the walking lunge come from how it challenges us while in motion,” says Samuel. “In addition to building strength and muscle, every step forward challenges your front leg (primarily tibailis and quad muscles) to decelerate your body in space, and then quickly work to accelerate into the next step. That’s building coordination and balance, in addition to training almost every lower-body muscle and building serious strength.”

You’ll work a number of major leg muscles when you do walking lunges, including your calves, hamstrings, quads, and glutes.

SMALL MISTAKES IN your walking lunge technique can turn the lower body exercise into a potential knee-wrecking disaster.

You want to land on the heel of your foot first to provide a strong base for the rest of your lunge position. When you get started with walking lunges, aim for a vertical shin as you lower down to the ground to stay at a 90-degree angle in your front and back legs.

You also don’t want to think of taking a step forward, but stepping out a couple inches by slightly turning your glute. Another adjustment to protect your knee is to shift your knee slightly outward instead of toward the midline. (If you still feel any knee pain during lunges, try a reverse lunge instead).

Keep your torso straight and avoid dipping forward, which you may be more inclined to do if you’re carrying heavy weights for this exercise. Your chest should be aligned with the back of your thigh the entire time. As you get up from the lunge, you want to avoid using momentum. That means no shoulder or torso rocking.

THE WALKING LUNGE is a great way to sneak in some movement on leg day if most of your lower-body exercises have both feet anchored to the ground. Load up some weights, and try to aim for 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg, 1 to 2 times a week. You can alternate each leg or finish up all your reps on one leg before switching to the other. Samuel says that will keep more tension and gives you an opportunity to really focus on the muscle.

An advantage of this move is its versatility, allowing you to do it anytime, anywhere. If you’re crunched for time or in a hotel room, try bodyweight walking lunges. Do it for 45 seconds with a 15 second rest for 5 minutes to break a sweat and build muscle.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., is the fitness director of Men's Health and a certified trainer with more than 10 years of training experience. He's logged training time with NFL athletes and track athletes and his current training regimen includes weight training, HIIT conditioning, and yoga. Before joining Men's Health, he served as a sports columnist and tech columnist for the New York Daily News.

#5043. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok Helped Plan Terror Attacks in Government Tests

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok Helped Plan Terror Attacks in Government Tests

Four of the most widely used AI chatbots helped government investigators develop potentially deadly attack plans in less than 12 hours, despite safeguards intended to stop exactly that kind of request.

OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Grok all supplied usable information during covert testing by the Government Accountability Office, according to a report released Wednesday. Investigators posed as attackers, then checked the responses against real locations, available materials, and expert assessments.

Two systems assisted with plans involving improvised explosives in crowded U.S. cities. Two others supplied information for attacks on electrical infrastructure, according to the watchdog, which withheld the models' assignments and operational details to prevent copycat attempts.

Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the investigation, warned that a terrorist could obtain "a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack" in less than 12 hours, according to her statement.

The chatbots initially activated protections, including refusing requests, removing harmful information or suspending accounts. Investigators bypassed those barriers with common jailbreak techniques, which manipulate an AI system into ignoring its safety rules.

The GAO checked suggested locations, researched whether materials were available and consulted specialists about the plans' feasibility. Some answers contained errors, including misplaced roads on a map, and investigators did not construct explosives or execute an attack.

In the report, "viable" means somebody would likely be able to follow the information supplied, not that an attack was demonstrated to succeed. Each model was tested on one assigned scenario, and the agency said the results were not statistically representative or suitable for ranking the companies.

OpenAI and Google said the tests involved older models, while Anthropic acknowledged that determined users can sometimes extract harmful material. The companies described continuing improvements to safety systems, though the GAO concluded those protections failed in its tests.

This is not really new. The findings follow a previous research showing eight of 10 popular chatbots assisted simulated teenage users planning violent attacks. The separate study tested 720 responses and found the bots provided actionable help roughly three-quarters of the time.

The GAO findings arrive amid outages affecting banks, Microsoft services and the National Security Agency. Officials say the disruptions were separate incidents, not evidence of a coordinated AI-driven cyberattack, even as the rush to repair software flaws has created its own problems.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton connected the NSA's outage to patching work. Officials described the recent breakdowns as maintenance-related, although individual organizations offered different explanations for their failures.

AI tools now find vulnerabilities faster than human teams can test and deploy fixes. Last month, the AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP flaws pushed website operators into an urgent patching campaign; the software powers a large share of the web.

The sheer volume is becoming another problem. VulnCheck data reveals there have been more than 100,000 software vulnerabilities logged this year by November 13, more than twice the total for 2025. Engineers still have to evaluate and deploy fixes without breaking the systems they are meant to protect.

That acceleration cuts both ways. Defenders gain powerful tools for finding weaknesses, but hasty repairs can disrupt essential systems, and malicious users may gain faster access to attack planning.

Hassan said she will make AI safety legislation an early priority when she takes over the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January. She plans hearings examining risks to public safety and critical infrastructure; the GAO itself made no formal policy recommendations.

#5040. Bitcoin Price Slips Near $61,500 as Tech Selloff Spreads to Asia

The bitcoin price slipped to near $61,500 on Friday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a selloff in technology stocks that followed Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut spread to Asian markets and dragged bitcoin to its lowest level since July.

Bitcoin first broke below $62,000 on Thursday evening, after Thursday afternoon’s report showed it giving back a rebound toward $64,000. The bitcoin price then slid to nearly $61,200 during Asian trading before bouncing back above $61,700. Friday marks a third straight day of losses.

The selling started in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi slid more than 5%, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics down around 6%. The Korea Exchange halted program selling for five minutes after the drop, while Japan’s Nikkei fell as much as 4.85% to a seven-month low.

U.S. futures pointed lower too. Nasdaq-100 futures fell more than 1.7% and S&P 500 futures dropped 0.8%, Yahoo Finance reported. Gold futures lost 3%. The S&P 500 is pointing to a seventh straight daily decline, its longest losing streak since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

Anthropic shares fell 8% in premarket trading after closing their first session at $97.17, up 17% from the $83 IPO price. Nvidia was down about 2.4% and AMD fell nearly 7%, CNBC reported. Hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials this week also weighed on sentiment, Reuters said.

Bitcoin funds are feeling the pressure. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $541.1 million in net outflows on Thursday, its largest single-day outflow since launch. That topped the previous record of $528.3 million set on Jan. 30. The fund bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows earlier this month.

Leveraged traders took heavy losses as the bitcoin price broke support. Bitcoin liquidations hit $712.9 million over 24 hours, with $614 million coming from long positions. Open interest in bitcoin futures fell to $18 billion from $20 billion a week ago, and funding rates flipped broadly negative as traders unwound their bets.

Traders are now watching whether the bitcoin price can hold the $60,000 area. A large pocket of long positions sits in the $60,500 to $60,900 band, just below the current price, and could come into play on a further drop. Bitcoin is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022.

Crypto stocks pointed lower in premarket trading. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $83.90, down about 2.6% from Thursday’s close of $86.13, after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 2.7% to near $106.

Bitcoin miners fell harder. IREN (IREN) dropped about 4.4%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 3.6% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 3.4%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 3.3%. IREN has also been under pressure as investors reassess AI infrastructure stocks. Delays in bringing some of its capacity online led Microsoft to spend less with the miner than planned last quarter.

Longer-term buyers have not left entirely. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market for bitcoin to date, putting the drawdown at around 54% compared with declines of more than 70% in previous cycles.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,800.

#5039. Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

The tampered Ledger wallets aren’t just a Southeast Asia problem anymore.

Ledger said Wednesday it has confirmed tampered hardware wallets in Berlin and is investigating reports of two more in Dubai, expanding a probe it had previously described as a localized incident in Southeast Asia.

“Our findings since then show tampered devices outside Southeast Asia. It is the same incident,” the company said in an update on its support site.

The investigation began last month after customers who bought devices from reseller CryptoBilis reported losses. Onchain investigators traced a suspected drain of about $87 million from hundreds of victim wallets across Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin.

Ledger said at the time that all confirmed cases were tied to CryptoBilis, and it later asked resellers in seven Asian markets to pull devices from sale.

Every device Ledger has confirmed shows the same kind of physical modification, designed to capture a user’s recovery phrase during setup. A recovery phrase, typically a string of 24 words, is the master key to a crypto wallet: anyone who has it can drain the funds.

Our investigation into the hardware implant incident we disclosed Oct 15th is ongoing, and we published an update: https://t.co/wx6mfQPr99

There is no flaw in Ledger's secure chip or operating system, and no confirmed case involving a device bought on https://t.co/vQ4QWa1D0f

Ledger maintains there’s no flaw in its secure chip or operating system and no confirmed case involving a device bought on ledger.com.

In Germany, Ledger said a few tampered units were localized to Berlin, and it urged anyone who bought a Ledger device there since January 2026 to contact support.

In Dubai, it’s working with distribution partners to learn how two suspected units entered circulation. Those devices were bought at a Virgin Megastore location, according to multiple reports. Ledger also found one affected Nano Gen5 among the Southeast Asian resellers it previously paused.

The company expects more tampered devices to surface, though it says the number remains small overall. Its Donjon security team is examining suspected devices, and Ledger has asked resellers to pause sales wherever inspections are ongoing.

Customers worried about a device should stop using it, Ledger said. It advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a device bought directly from ledger.com, without reusing the old recovery phrase or passphrase, since a tampered device can capture both. It also recommends filing a report with local authorities.

For a limited time, Ledger is offering physical inspections, including X-rays, at its factory in Vierzon, France.

“We will never ask for your recovery phrase,” the company said on X.

The last few months have been a rough stretch for hardware wallet markers overall. Rival manufacturer Trezor said this week that hackers who breached a third-party shipping partner likely took information tied to about 27,000 orders. That’s the company’s third such breach in as many months.

In general, aim for a bench that can support at least 500 pounds; that'll set you up for success in nearly all your training and support more advanced exercises that bring even more impact (such as step-ups and plyometric Bulgarians).

The right balance between stiff and cushioned padding is essential to ensure your bench will stay in good condition with use. Highly cushioned benches might feel nice, but they tend to deform over time, creating an uneven surface. This can also compromise your form during workouts, especially when your spine or shoulders are required to stay in alignment. While most padding is stitched to the bench, some is stapled, which tends to lift away from the bench’s frame eventually. Not enough padding isn't good either, as you'll feel like you're lying on a plywood board.

If you plan on using your adjustable bench for flat bench variations, be mindful of the distance between the back pad and seat pad (otherwise known as the ‘pad gap’). Anything larger than 2 inches will be noticeable and may feel uncomfortable during certain lifts.

In general, the three types of weight benches are flat, adjustable incline, and adjustable incline/decline. The first two are pretty self-explanatory and the latter, of course, adds versatility for decline-angle exercises. "If you're unsure which bench to get, opt for a bench with incline-angle options. Sure, this may cost slightly more initially, but it'll set you up with a bench that can grow with you," explains Samuel. "In general, most website workouts and app workouts assume that, if you're training with a bench, it has incline options. So not having incline options can set you up for frustration. It'll also heavily limit your ability to vary your workouts in fun ways. The incline bench is the most future-proofed purchase option."

If you're a powerlifter, or you're buying a bench for a particular program, a flat bench might be perfect. Decline-angle benches open up new movements (especially when it comes to core training), but they're generally unnecessary. Think of that as your luxury option.

Like all home gym equipment, weight benches can take up a lot of room. If you’re tight on space or just appreciate being able to move your equipment out of the way, consider a collapsible weight bench or, at the very least, one with wheels. If you’re after an adjustable weight bench, wheels should be a top priority. Because they’re on the heavier side, this will make stowing away and setting up tremendously easier. You don't want setting up your bench every session to be a part of your workout.

Return policies and warranties represent the manufacturer’s confidence in its product. And with most home gym equipment manufacturers, the better the quality, the better the warranty. In the case that something goes wrong with your bench, it’s important to know your investment is protected, so look for benches that come with at least a one-year warranty.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, my job is to evaluate the latest and greatest training equipment available. I've had extensive experience with weight benches in both the training facilities I've worked out of and the home gyms I've built. I also consulted with Men's Health fitness experts, editors, and writers on the top weight benches they’ve experienced firsthand. The experts included our own Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. The team has tested dozens of weight benches over the years, from high-end, commercial-grade models to budget options.

Our extensive testing process involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors—including size, durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value—to ensure that we recommend only the best. We tested each weight bench through exercise routines that included flat and adjustable bench moves, covering a wide range of motions and use scenarios. To determine stability and structural integrity, we tested benches at both comfortable and near-maximum capacities, allowing us to assess performance under varying loads.

To gather diverse perspectives, we consulted with our MH Advisory Board and Strength in Diversity trainers, who provided valuable feedback on the top weight benches based on their expertise and experiences. The result is the picks for the best weight benches you can buy right now.

You don’t necessarily need a weight bench to get strong and build muscle, but having one gives you access to a host of exercises (regardless of fitness level), especially when it comes to upper-body training.

Most basic exercises that beginners should master, like dumbbell presses and single-arm dumbbell rows and hip thrusts, are much easier to execute with a bench (especially an adjustable one). Meanwhile, more advanced lifters can get incredible mileage out of a bench by unlocking more innovative moves like half-bench single-arm presses and single-arm rows.

Here's a breakdown of the key differences:

A flat weight bench is designed with a fixed, flat surface, whereas an adjustable weight bench allows you to adjust the angle of the bench to different incline or, in some cases, decline angles.

"The adjustable benches that offer a decline setting are a terrific value for anyone who wants to get creative with their core exercises while training at home," says Samuel.

"Adjustable benches give you so many more options for your exercises," explains David Otey, C.S.C.S and Men's Health Advisory Board member. "Instead of just working at flat or upright, all of the angles in between can give you variety and diversity in your training options." Those angles allow you to bias muscle groups in different, more selective ways. A flat weight bench limits you to exercises that can be performed on a flat surface.

Adjustable benches offer more convenience overall (especially well-built ones), offering access to more movements and angles. Adjustable benches also offer support for extra movements, such as overhead presses and lateral raises, which can allow for greater loading of those movements in the long term. But flat weight benches win for convenience in two areas. They're generally lighter, so you can more easily move them around your gym, and they're easier to stow when not in use, too.

Because flat weight benches generally have fewer mechanisms and lack a hinge of any sort, they'll be easier to maintain. Adjustable benches don't require a ton of maintenance, but it's worthwhile every so often to check on bolts and caps, and make sure your hinge mechanism is working smoothly.

We consulted with Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., for the best exercises for beginners to get the most out of a weight bench.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., is the fitness director of Men's Health and a certified trainer with more than 10 years of training experience. He's logged training time with NFL athletes and track athletes and his current training regimen includes weight training, HIIT conditioning, and yoga. #5036. Bitcoin Hovers Just Above Average Holder’s Cost Basis as Price Keeps Dipping

Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday.

The price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000. The realized price is a measure of what holders paid, not where the market trades. When bitcoin trades above it, the typical coin is sitting on a gain. Below it, the typical coin is underwater.

The margin is thin. The firm said the MVRV ratio, which compares bitcoin’s market value with its realized value, sits “just above 1.” A reading of 1 means the market price has fallen all the way to the realized price.

Realized price values each coin at the price it last moved on the blockchain, then averages across the supply. Look Into Bitcoin describes it as bitcoin’s average cost basis. Because it tracks the price when coins last changed hands, it moves far more slowly than the market.

The MVRV ratio expresses the same idea as a multiple. Above 1, holders are in profit on average. Below 1, they are not. A reading just above 1 means the market price is only a sliver higher than what the average coin cost.

The firm did not give the exact realized price in its post, which included a chart. That leaves the exact cushion between today’s price and the average cost basis unstated. Bitcoin Magazine Pro’s full realized price chart sits behind a login, so the current level could not be confirmed independently for this report.

“The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit,” the firm wrote. “The margin is thin.”

The slide has come with heavy selling from funds. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost about $541 million on Thursday, its largest one-day outflow since it launched in January 2024, Bloomberg reported. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total that day.

The selling stands out against the buying earlier in the fall. Institutions piled into bitcoin ETFs through the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record, Bitcoin Magazine reported this week.

Leveraged traders took losses too. More than $700 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, and about 86% of them were bets on higher prices. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $200 million of the total.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the drop is part of a longer downturn rather than the start of a new one. “I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another,” he said in a note dated Nov. 18.

The note frames Friday’s price action as a late stage of a decline that began well before November. Butterfill pointed to whale selling that weighed on prices from late 2025, expectations of higher interest rates and weakness in technology stocks, all of which have kept buyers cautious.

“Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he said. “Geopolitics will have a considerable say in that.”

A move through the realized price would put bitcoin near the bottom edge of that range. The firm said holders as a group have not been in loss since early 2023.

A sustained breakout, Butterfill said, would likely require “a change in the policy outlook, renewed whale participation or both.”

#5033. The 8 Best Electric Razors for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHOEVER SAID PATIENCE is a virtue did not have facial hair, or at least, they weren’t regularly shaving it. Even as Men’s Health’s Grooming Editor, I’m usually running behind and rushing through my shave routine, whether I’m packing my traveling grooming essentials, deciding what toiletries to bring camping, or just trying to get to work. If it weren’t for electric razors, I would have committed to a life of looking like Charles Darwin long ago.

Of course, there are plenty of reasons punctual guys might want to use an electric razor in lieu of traditional cartridge razors. These shavers are gentler on skin, gliding across the face with less direct blade contact to reduce irritation and minimize the risk of nicks and cuts. They also help prevent razor bumps and burns by trimming hair above the surface instead of dragging against the skin like traditional razors do.

To be clear, it takes skin a few sessions to get used to shaving with these devices if you’ve been a long-time cartridge devotee. This is because electric razors move differently and do not cut as close, so your skin needs time to adapt to the new sensation and technique. Also, switching razors changes how the blades interact with your skin, which can cause temporary irritation as your skin builds tolerance.

Still, these tools streamline the whole process: they're fast, easy to use, and travel-friendly since you don’t need to pack extra products, like shaving cream. Many models even come with smart features like pressure sensors and AI, making them more intuitive and unique to the user. Most you can use wet or dry, with or without shaving cream, and they're versatile enough for your face, head, or body. Plus, some have add-ons that can help you replace multiple grooming tools, simplify your routine, and free up space on your bathroom shelf.

But regardless of why you’re using an electric razor, the biggest thing is finding the right one for you. The good news is that no matter what your budget, skin or hair type, or grooming acumen, there's an electric razor that will suit your needs.

Braun electric razors have been a favorite of Men’s Health since we first launched our grooming vertical in 2018. For years, we maintained that the Braun Series 9 Pro was in a class of its own when it came to electric shavers. Then, the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus was released, which took these tools to an entirely new level.

At first glance, the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus looks almost identical to the original Series 9—and that’s not a bad thing. It keeps the same ergonomic design, which strikes a near-perfect balance in the hand: lightweight enough to maneuver easily, yet hefty enough to feel secure while shaving. Like its predecessor, the Pro Plus features five cutting elements that trim hairs down to an ultra-smooth 0.05 mm, giving you that just-shaved feel with impressive precision that’s as close as you’ll get without using an old-school barbershop blade.

Where it really starts to separate itself from the previous model, and any other electric razor for that matter, is the blades. The OG version’s blades were titanium, but the Pro Plus blades are made from surgical-grade stainless steel that stay sharper, allowing for a more effective shave that lasts longer. The Braun Series 9 Pro Plus, like the original version, features an ultra-thin ProLift blade (which looks like a gold bar on the razor head itself) that helps to lift hair away from your skin for a thorough cut.

What Else to Consider: Despite all that praise, the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus doesn’t lead the pack in terms of raw motor speed. It clocks in at 40,000 cutting actions per minute, which is solid but far from the top. But similar to Draymond Green’s career stats, the numbers don’t tell the whole story—this delivers the most powerful shave on the market. Sure, the Philips Norelco Shaver 9800 boasts a much faster motor (up to 150,000-cuts-per-minute), but speed isn’t everything.

What sets the Series 9 Pro Plus apart is Braun’s Sonic Technology, which adds 10,000 micro-vibrations per minute on top of the motor's output. These vibrations help lift and capture more hair with each pass, making every stroke more effective and efficient. The razor also features a pop-up trimmer and a flexing head, which performed especially well compared to the Panasonic Arc5.

Its pivoting head perfectly hugs facial contours with more precision, likely due to its slightly smaller, more agile design. It also includes the AI-driven ProSensoAdapt, which senses beard density 300 times per second, according to the brand. This automatically adjusts power in real time for a smoother, more personalized shave.

Why We Chose It: Shaving with the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus rarely takes more than five minutes, even less when my stubble is light, but its standout feature is the incredibly close shave it delivers. The innovative focus is on lifting hairs more effectively from the skin to ensure a smoother finish.

Another feature I didn’t know I needed from an electric razor is the ProComfort pre-shave head, which gently lifts and prepares hairs for a closer, more comfortable shave. It does this by using fine, vibrating blades to raise and align hairs before the main shaver cuts them.

These upgrades make a real difference. It’s by far the closest shave I get from an electric razor, especially when I use the ProComfort head beforehand to prep my skin. No other tool gets me this close to 5 o'clock before the shadow shows up.

Long-Term Results: I’ve been using my Braun Series 9 Pro Plus for over a year, and it still shaves just as well today as it did right out of the box. Overall performance has not changed, though there has been a slight decline in cutting power when the blade dulled. But replacing the head was easy and brought the shaver back to business immediately.

Another Men’s Health shaving staple, especially for those with sensitive skin. You’d expect a razor this powerful to cause irritation, especially considering its five (incredibly sharp) blades, but it doesn’t. The Arc5 shaves nearly as close as any manual razor and cream combo I’ve used, and the pivoting head effortlessly glides over tricky areas like my neck and jawline without missing a spot.

Despite its impressive performance, the device feels light in the hand and operates super quietly; it’s barely loud enough for you to realize it’s on. While it doesn’t match the Braun Series 9’s extras like AI-powered shave sensors that adjust to beard density, I’ve still found this simpler version more than capable. It gives a clean, close shave without any fuss.

What Else to Consider: With a wide head and a strong motor, this shaver is powerful. It boasts 55,000-cuts-per-minute—more than the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus but less than the absurd Norelco 9800 150,000-cuts-per-minute motor. Even if you don’t have sensitive skin, go easy until you get the hang of how much to press the foil against your face.

Like Davante Adams in the middle of the field, the Arc5 cuts fast. Still, don’t rush through shave jobs, as this can cause some irritation if you’re not careful, no matter the device you’re using. Once you get the hang of it, though, it minimizes the amount of time you have to shave the same area. Overall, it is slightly bulkier than the closest similar razor (Braun Series 9) and has a shorter battery life (45 minutes versus 60 minutes), which could come down to the fact that it’s just a larger device in general.

The Panasonic Arc5’s blades are hypoallergenic, as they’re made from surgical-grade stainless steel that resists corrosion, minimizes skin reactions, and maintains a smooth, low-friction surface, all of which makes it ideal for dealing with sensitive skin. Additionally, the foils covering the blades are designed to be gentle and smooth, which further helps protect the skin from irritation or razor burn.

Why We Chose It: In addition to convenience, the biggest draw of electric razors is that they’re much gentler on skin, helping avoid the razor bumps and irritation that come with close manual shaves. What stands out to me about this model is how closely it shaves—nearly as close as a traditional wet razor, yet without the usual irritation.

After the few shaves it took for my skin to adapt, I noticed a significant drop in bumps. It’s a powerful, efficient tool that’s straightforward and intuitive with no unnecessary features to complicate things. For anyone with sensitive skin, this razor is easily the most skin-friendly option I’ve tried, and it delivers smooth results without the harsh aftermath.

Long-Term Results: The Arc5 holds up over time. After months of use, the cutting power has not decreased a bit, and post-shave irritation remains a rare occurrence. The blades are as sharp and gentle as they were out of the box.

For anyone constantly battling stubborn neck hairs, this is the razor for you. The Norelco 9800 brings AI into the shaving routine to deliver an impressively close and precise shave. Its rotary heads easily follow facial contours, while built-in pressure sensors give real-time feedback, letting you know when they’re applying too much or too little pressure.

Powered by Dual Steel Precision blades, which are two layers of self‑sharpening stainless steel blades that increase cutting speed and efficiency, making up to 150,000 cuts per minute. This razor doesn’t leave a single stray hair behind.

With 72 rotating blades offering full 360-degree movement, it seamlessly adapts to every curve of the face. To top it off, the smart companion app tracks shaving patterns and offers personalized tips for better technique, making this one of the most advanced grooming tools on the market.

What Else to Consider: The Norelco 9800 blows every other rotary shaver out of the water. Not only is the motor by far the most powerful (again, 150,000-cuts-per-minute!), but the three-head design offers a great range of motion, allowing for more pivoting and a closer shave around the contours of your face. The blades on the 9800 also have a micro-bead coating to help reduce irritation, which we found helpful.

Though not usually a huge tech junkie, I recommend using the app to change the settings, especially if you use it wet or dry, because adjusting those settings manually can be difficult. That being said, it does take a bit of time to adjust to your style of shaving. It’s a bit overly responsive at first, so when you first apply more pressure in less sensitive areas, like your cheeks, it can overcompensate when moving to areas like the curves in your neck and lead to nicks. However, it quickly adjusted after a couple of uses.

Why We Chose It: If it's features you want, this electric razor is chock-full of them. AI helps guide your shaving to create the best shave you can possibly get, as long as you use those features to their full advantage. If you don’t, you’ll still get a good, close shave, but this thing really sings when everything works together. Similar to Braun’s AI, the 9800 senses hair density and automatically adjusts; however, it also provides real-time pressure feedback via the light ring and connected app.

Long-Term Results: This definitely proved to be for the type of guy who likes to tinker and customize, and I can appreciate that. Of all the rotary-head razors I’ve tested, this one flexed and pivoted to the shape of my face the best without missing too many spots. Furthermore, the cleaning and charging station is the sleekest and simplest on the market, and I always appreciate space-saving.

My favorite thing about the Chairman Plus is how streamlined the design is. Sure, there are a handful of nifty gadgets and features, like the travel lock, SkinSafe blade protection, and ergonomic grip, but none are excessive. More than anything, however, they’re all functional.

So often with grooming devices, they tend to sound exciting or interesting, but when put into practice, they’re either overly complicated or straight-up unnecessary. That’s not the case with The Chairman Plus, as every feature was clearly designed to simplify the shaving experience and make it as easy as possible.

What Else to Consider: Of all the practical design boons of this trimmer, the most notable is also the simplest: its grip. Thanks to an innovative (albeit uncomplicated) ergonomic design, this shaver is the easiest to hold and use on this list. Contrary to the Chairman Pro's more straight horizontal handle, the Plus features a slight indent on each side under the razor head to create more of a T-shape than the traditional V-shape.

I have been known to drop razors mid-job from time to time, so I found this a welcome update that creates a much easier-to-hold grip. It’s ideal for clumsy people like me or those new to electric shavers in general.

Why We Chose It: Ultimately, this selection came down to how easy this razor is to use, along with how gentle it is on skin. If you’re new to electric razors or shaving in general, the Chairman Plus represents a low-risk introduction to these tools. At barely over a pound, it’s super lightweight, and its SkinSafe-protected blades, which feature a built-in safety guard between sets of rounded (rather than harsher straight ones) stainless steel blades, make cuts and tugs few and far between. While the shave isn’t as close as other options on this list, sans the OneBlade, it’s one of the more gentle and certainly the best for beginners.

Long-Term Results: I really dig the travel lock on this device; it’s simple to use, but also takes some effort to click on and off. This helped me avoid accidentally turning it on when traveling and slicing through other products or ruining clothes packed near it (did I mention the clumsiness?). Again, it doesn’t give the closest shave, but that’s not always the most important thing if you have sensitive skin, like I do, and would rather avoid irritation (which this does).

If you’re looking for the closest trim without completely shaving your beard (like a slight five-o’clock shadow), this easy-to-use electric shaver is a top choice. It's great for trimming the hair on your face, neck, and basically any other area without worrying about nicks and cuts. You can easily achieve the perfect length of scruff with three combs and a contoured head that moves to the shape of your face.

What Else to Consider: Unlike the other electric razors on this list, the Philips Norelco OneBlade is more of a multi-use gadget. It shaves, and it trims. The blade is a completely different design from the linear blades of the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus or the rotary blades of the Norelco 9800, yet it shaves effectively and closely (though not as close as those two options, to be clear).

The motor is also weak in comparison (12,000 cuts per minute), but it’s ideal for cutting any length of hair. If you’re the type of guy who likes to vary up his facial hair look, you can use this razor to keep it in check without needing to switch between multiple tools.

As someone who was once deeply committed to old-school blades, I appreciate how this handles like a traditional razor, thanks to an ergonomic design and classically shaped handle, but you can’t treat it exactly the same as your typical razor.

There's a bit of a learning curve to understand how hard to press it and how to move it around your face to get the best shave. It also won’t ever completely shave as close as a more typical electric razor. It always leaves a slight amount of stubble, so if you’re looking for a baby-smooth shave, this might not be for you.

Why We Chose It: The Philips Norelco OneBlade easily ranks among the most innovative grooming tools I’ve used. It’s lightweight, sleek, and shaped like a classic razor, so using it feels totally natural. No matter your facial hair type, it delivers a smooth, easy cut. What really sets it apart is the included adjustable five-length comb.

I use it not just for clean shaves, but also for trimming and shaping my beard, and even body hair (with a separate blade to keep things hygienic). Best part? It fits right into my Dopp kit—no bulky case needed. It's a perfect travel companion without taking up extra space in my bag.

Long-Term Results: In terms of sheer versatility, the Philips Norelco OneBlade can’t be beat. It may not be the most powerful or closest shaver on the market, but if you know that going in and use it accordingly, it exceeds expectations in terms of function. I’ve used it on my face, neck, body (after switching the blade, of course), and anywhere else I need to trim or shave. Plus, did I mention it's less than 40 bucks?

A few of the electric razors on this list come with stellar travel cases, like the Braun 9 or OG Arc5, but let’s be real—these will take up a lot of space in your bag. If you’re committed to only traveling with a carry-on or just want more space for other things, these cases are going to prove to be a nuisance.

This is why the Panasonic Arc5 Palm-Sized Electric Razor won a 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award. Now, this design can make the actual shaving experience a bit awkward (especially the first few times you use it), because of how you have to hold the tool. But once you get the hang of it, it’s pretty easy to accomplish. And for the space you’ll be saving from using it, it’ll be worth the few more minutes it takes to get the shave job done.

While I wouldn’t necessarily recommend using this as an everyday razor (grab the original Arc5 for that), it’s powered by a 13,000-cuts-per-minute motor, so you could certainly do worse if you’re a heavy traveler and don’t want to splurge on multiple devices. Still, while these blades cut nearly as powerfully as the original version’s 15,000 cuts per minute, the blade head is smaller, so it will take some extra time. Why We Chose It: With 50 minutes of use from one charge, you might not even need to pack the cord if you’re traveling less than a full week. Long-Term Results: I’ve been lugging this thing around for months on various trips, and the motor hasn’t let up one bit. It still holds that near-hour charge, and the blades feel just as sharp. I may never pack a full-sized electric razor again.

The blade type is a key factor to consider when choosing an electric razor. You’ll typically choose between two main options: rotary blades and foil blades.

If you usually let your stubble grow out or don’t shave every day, a rotary electric razor is your best bet. Its circular motion and flexible head follow the curves of your face, helping it cut through longer or more uneven hair with ease. Rotary razors work especially well for those with normal to tougher skin and medium to coarse beard density, offering a comfortable and efficient shave even after a few days of growth.

A foil works best for shorter facial hair or when you're aiming for a close shave similar to classic razors. It uses oscillating blades hidden beneath a thin, perforated foil that captures and cuts hairs as they emerge through the mesh. While a foil shaver tends to be noisier than rotary models, it offers deeper precision. To get the smoothest results, use it with straight, steady strokes—moving back and forth along the face and neck. This design makes foil razors ideal for those who shave daily or want clean, sharp lines around facial hair.

Corded razors plug directly into a power source, so you don’t have to worry about charging or replacing batteries. As a result, they deliver more consistent power and longer performance. Since they don’t need to conserve energy, they also usually run stronger than cordless models. That said, cordless razors offer added convenience, especially for travel or grooming on the go, with options powered by either rechargeable or disposable batteries. Ultimately, the right choice depends on your routine and how much flexibility you need.

Many premium models offer additional features or accessories to enhance the shave experience or make it more convenient, including:

The Men’s Health grooming team has been extensively testing electric razors since 2018. For years, we’ve been putting shavers to the test, evaluating their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use over long periods of time. As someone who can get a five o'clock shadow before lunch, I am constantly shaving. This has given me a consistent canvas to test and retest editor favorites, as well as the latest innovations and new grooming releases.

For this story, I considered the team’s reviews and notes of top-performing razors dating back eight years, in addition to my own experience, to land on 15 options to extensively test or retest over an 18-month trial period. I’ve also included before-and-after shots of yours truly for most of the razors to show the kind of shave each one delivers. Based on this first-hand use, I narrowed that list to eight, representing the best electric razors for men to buy in 2026.

Both electric and manual razors use blades to cut hair, but they do it in different ways. Manual razors pull each hair up with the first blade, then slice it closer to the skin with the following blades—kind of like using a knife. Electric razors, on the other hand, work more like scissors. Most use a foil system: hair enters tiny holes in the foil, and internal blades cut it from beneath. Rotary versions use a slightly different mechanism, but the concept is similar.

Manual razors shave closer because the blades touch the skin directly. That closeness comes with a downside: higher chances of razor burn, bumps, or ingrown hairs, especially if you skip proper prep or use a dull blade. Electric razors always have a barrier between the blade and skin, so while they won’t shave quite as close, they’re often gentler and better suited for sensitive skin.

Read More: 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Awards

Using an electric razor is much easier to pick up compared to a traditional or safety razor. Still, don’t just grab yours and start shaving right away. Take the time to learn how to get the closest shave possible before speeding through the process for the best results.

Start your shave with clean skin. Whether you’re using a wet or dry shaver, you should tackle your scruff right after washing your face. For dry shavers, apply a small amount of pre-shave oil or wash your face and then gently pat it dry. These shavers perform best when the stubble is firm and completely dry.

Keep the razor at a 90-degree angle to your skin to avoid cutting hairs unevenly. There’s no need to press hard, as a light grip does the job. Pressing down too much, especially around the jaw or chin, can lead to patchy results and irritation. With a foil shaver, I stick to back-and-forth strokes. If I’m using a rotary, I’ll go with either circular or straight motions, depending on what feels best.

Reading the manual might seem unnecessary (and boring), but brands often include specific tips or techniques tailored to their design. Those little details can make a big difference, resulting in a noticeably smoother shave. It might not be Hemingway, but taking a few minutes to go through the instructions usually pays off in better results and a more comfortable experience overall.

As long as I stick to proper maintenance and care, I get a consistently smooth shave from electric razors. If you’re new to these tools, however, give your skin about two weeks to adjust—it makes a big difference. A little patience and upkeep go a long way.

One of the first things I check in an electric razor is how easy it is to clean because this will help both its effectiveness and longevity (not to mention my blood pressure). Skipping regular cleaning can clog the blades with hair and gunk, which not only affects performance but also shortens the razor’s life. When using a waterproof device, I always rinse mine under running water after each use, then use a small brush to clear out any buildup on the foil.

That foil is key to getting a smooth, even shave, but it’s delicate. If it gets bent or damaged, replace it right away. Letting it go risks rough shaves, irritation, or even breakouts from dragging dirt across your skin. Some higher-end models, like the Braun Series 9, come with automatic cleaning stations. They’re super convenient (even if a bit bulky and noisy) and use replaceable cartridges that last around three months—about $5 each in a multi-pack. While not essential, they definitely make it easier to stay on top of maintenance.

Read More: How To Maintain Your Beard Trimmer

High-quality electric razors—especially those in the $200-plus range—can last years, sometimes even five or more if well maintained. To keep mine running strong, I make sure to replace the blades and foil regularly. Depending on the brand, blade replacement is usually recommended every 6 to 18 months. I also keep an eye on the foil. If it gets dented or damaged, I swap it out immediately since most replacement cartridges include both parts.

These typically cost between $20 and $50. Battery life is typically the first thing to go. Over time, even the best razors start to lose their charge faster or run with less power. When I notice my shave isn’t as close, or the razor starts pulling instead of cutting cleanly, that’s my cue that it might be time for a new one.
